home.preset.title: Load-test presets (by target capacity)
home.preset.hint: Pick the CPU, memory, and bandwidth tier closest to your site to fill in reference concurrency, duration, and timeout. Lower concurrency for large pages or slow APIs.
home.preset.starter.name: Starter host
home.preset.starter.rationale: For personal blogs, static sites, or shared hosting. At 1 Mbps, a 50 KB page sustains roughly 2 RPS; 5 concurrent users simulates a short spike without instantly saturating CPU or egress. 30 seconds is enough to spot trends; a 15s timeout tolerates cold starts and slow queries.
home.preset.basic.name: Light cloud VM
home.preset.basic.rationale: For small WordPress sites or corporate homepages. Two cores support about 10 worker threads; 5 Mbps fits roughly 5–10 RPS depending on page size. 45 seconds yields stable latency percentiles; a 12s timeout covers occasional slow dynamic responses.
home.preset.standard.name: Standard cloud VM
home.preset.standard.rationale: For mid-size sites and light APIs. ~5 concurrent connections per core → 20 total, aligned with 10 Mbps at ~100 KB responses. 60 seconds is a common benchmark window for p90/p99; a 10s timeout matches typical web SLAs.
home.preset.growth.name: Growth tier
home.preset.growth.rationale: Extra RAM caches more connections and page fragments for rising traffic. 35 concurrent probes headroom before CPU saturates; 20 Mbps is rarely the first bottleneck. 60 seconds helps you see whether queues start building.
home.preset.enterprise.name: Enterprise host
home.preset.enterprise.rationale: Reference for multi-module apps or medium-traffic API nodes. Start around 60 concurrent and watch CPU and error rate before going higher; 50 Mbps supports higher RPS. 90 seconds can surface connection-pool exhaustion or slow leaks.
home.preset.performance.name: High-performance host
home.preset.performance.rationale: Capacity check for high-traffic portals or core API gateways. 100 concurrent is a moderate load per core (~6–7 each) to avoid hammering immediately. 120 seconds covers post-warmup steady state; an 8s timeout assumes an optimized service and focuses on tail latency.

report.rps.tip: RPS (Requests Per Second) measures throughput. For HTTP/API load tests, RPS is usually equivalent to QPS. Interpret together with latency and success rate.
report.latency.tip: A latency percentile shows what share of requests finished within a given time. For example, p90 = 200ms means 90% of requests returned within 200 milliseconds.
report.p50.tip: p50 (median): 50% of requests took this long or less. Represents typical user experience.
report.p90.tip: p90: 90% of requests took this long or less. Shows the slower tail for most users.
report.p95.tip: p95: 95% of requests took this long or less. Often used in SLA targets.
report.p99.tip: p99: 99% of requests took this long or less. Highlights tail latency and rare slow requests.
err.url_invalid: Invalid URL; must be http or https
err.url_ssrf: Private, loopback, and reserved targets are not allowed (SSRF protection)
err.inflight: Too many running jobs; try again later
suggest.low_success.title: Low success rate
suggest.low_success.detail: Success rate is below 95%. Check capacity, timeouts, and upstream stability.
suggest.tail_latency.title: High tail latency
suggest.tail_latency.detail: p99 is much higher than p50. Investigate slow queries, lock contention, GC pauses, and connection pool queues.
suggest.server_error.title: Many server errors
suggest.server_error.detail: Many 5xx responses. Inspect app and gateway logs for faults and resource exhaustion.
suggest.throttled.title: Throttling or overload
suggest.throttled.detail: Many 429/503 responses. Review rate limits, autoscaling, and degradation strategies.
suggest.connect_error.title: Connection errors elevated
suggest.connect_error.detail: Many DNS/connect/TLS failures. Check Keep-Alive, file descriptor limits, reverse proxies, and certificates.
suggest.slow_ok.title: Slow but mostly successful
suggest.slow_ok.detail: Most requests succeed but latency is high. Consider caching, CDN, compression, and backend profiling.
suggest.healthy.title: Looks healthy
suggest.healthy.detail: No alert thresholds were triggered. Keep watching peak traffic and capacity planning.
glossary.title: Load-test glossary
glossary.subtitle: Definitions of common abbreviations and metrics. For HTTP load tests, RPS and QPS are usually the same.
glossary.term.rps.title: RPS (Requests Per Second)
glossary.term.rps.body: HTTP requests handled per second. RPS = total requests ÷ elapsed seconds. For one HTTP call per operation, RPS matches QPS.
glossary.term.qps.title: QPS (Queries Per Second)
glossary.term.qps.body: Queries per second — common in search, databases, and caches. Often used interchangeably with RPS; strictly, QPS emphasizes read/query operations. This tool counts each HTTP request once; report RPS is QPS in that sense.
glossary.term.tps.title: TPS (Transactions Per Second)
glossary.term.tps.body: Business or database transactions per second. One transaction may involve multiple SQL or HTTP calls, so TPS is often ≤ RPS. This tool counts HTTP requests only, not TPS.
glossary.term.throughput.title: Throughput
glossary.term.throughput.body: Work completed per unit time — an umbrella term. Can mean RPS/QPS/TPS or bytes per second (B/s). This report shows RPS and bytes transferred as two throughput views.
glossary.term.latency.title: Latency
glossary.term.latency.body: Time from sending a request to receiving the full response, usually in milliseconds (ms). Includes network and server processing.
glossary.term.ttfb.title: TTFB (Time To First Byte)
glossary.term.ttfb.body: Time until the first response byte arrives — server processing plus network startup, excluding full body download. Helps tell server slowness from transfer slowness. This version reports total latency only, not TTFB separately.
glossary.term.success_rate.title: Success rate
glossary.term.success_rate.body: Share of requests that succeeded. This tool treats HTTP 2xx/3xx as success. Below 95% often signals overload or errors.
glossary.term.error_rate.title: Error rate
glossary.term.error_rate.body: Share of failed requests — the complement of success rate (≈ 100% − success rate). Includes timeouts, connection errors, and HTTP ≥400 responses.
glossary.term.p50.title: p50 (median)
glossary.term.p50.body: 50% of requests finished within this time — typical user experience.
glossary.term.p90.title: p90
glossary.term.p90.body: 90% of requests finished within this time — the slower but still common tail.
glossary.term.p95.title: p95
glossary.term.p95.body: 95% of requests finished within this time — often used in SLAs and capacity planning.
glossary.term.p99.title: p99
glossary.term.p99.body: 99% of requests finished within this time — highlights tail latency and rare slow requests.
glossary.term.concurrency.title: Concurrency
glossary.term.concurrency.body: Number of virtual users/workers sending requests at once. Higher concurrency increases load but may trigger throttling.
glossary.term.duration.title: Duration
glossary.term.duration.body: Total test length in seconds. Longer runs yield stabler percentiles but consume more target resources.
glossary.term.timeout.title: Timeout
glossary.term.timeout.body: Maximum wait time per request before it counts as failed. Increase for cold starts or slow dynamic pages.
glossary.term.ramp.title: Ramp-up
glossary.term.ramp.body: Gradually raises concurrency to the target over N seconds instead of hitting full load instantly. 0 means immediate full concurrency.
glossary.term.http.title: HTTP / HTTPS
glossary.term.http.body: Application protocols for the web. HTTPS adds TLS encryption. Only http and https targets are allowed.
glossary.term.status_code.title: HTTP status code
glossary.term.status_code.body: Three-digit server response code: 2xx success, 3xx redirect, 4xx client error, 5xx server error.
glossary.term.header.title: HTTP header
glossary.term.header.body: Key-value metadata on requests/responses, e.g. Authorization or Content-Type. Use custom headers to simulate auth or body types.
glossary.term.sse.title: SSE (Server-Sent Events)
glossary.term.sse.body: Server push to the browser over HTTP. Used here to stream live progress and chart data during a run.
glossary.term.sla.title: SLA (Service Level Agreement)
glossary.term.sla.body: Contracted service targets such as uptime or latency limits. Load tests help verify goals like p95 < 200ms.
glossary.term.ssrf.title: SSRF (Server-Side Request Forgery)
glossary.term.ssrf.body: Abuse where a server is tricked into requesting internal networks. Private/loopback targets are blocked to prevent misuse.
glossary.term.api.title: API (Application Programming Interface)
glossary.term.api.body: Programmatic interface, often HTTP JSON endpoints. Use POST body to load-test APIs.
glossary.term.cdn.title: CDN (Content Delivery Network)
glossary.term.cdn.body: Distributed cache of static assets closer to users, reducing latency and origin load.
